title: Reducing Barriers to Medical Use Licensing: proposed rule, 91 FR 47042
date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-07-27 (on-page Publication Date field: 07/27/2026; Published Document: 2026-15080 (91 FR 47042))
key_claim: The NRC proposes to remove the prescriptive classroom, laboratory and work-experience hour requirements in 10 CFR 35.190, 35.290, 35.390, 35.392, 35.394, 35.396, 35.490 and 35.690 for physicians who completed an accredited residency in a specialty where radiation safety is integrated, replacing hours with a residency pathway and preceptor attestation. It also eliminates the licence-amendment requirement for adding authorised users for diagnostic uses, broadens the definition of physician to include foreign-trained US-licensed doctors, and raises the decay-in-storage half-life ceiling from 120 to 275 days to cover Lu-177m and Co-57. The package is costed at $39.1 million undiscounted net savings over 2027-2031. The rule also records that in March 2016 the ACMUI found no evidence the 700-hour requirement adversely affected patient access.
frame_summary: The NRC is arguing that hour-based radiation-safety qualification rules are a disproportionate burden on already residency-trained physicians and that the administrative gate on adding authorised users can be devolved to licensees without loss of safety.
verbatim_quote: Specifically, the NRC proposes to remove the prescriptive requirements in §§ 35.190, 35.290, 35.390, 35.392, 35.394, 35.396, 35.490, and 35.690 for specific numbers of classroom, laboratory, and work experience hours for physicians who have completed residency training in specialties where radiation safety and the clinical use of byproduct material are inherently integrated into the curriculum.
verbatim_list: Over the 5-year analysis period (2027-2031), the proposed revisions are estimated to generate net savings of $39.1 million (savings minus costs), undiscounted.

Eliminating the requirement for license amendments to add authorized users for diagnostic uses, allowing licensees to approve and document these users internally due to the lower risk of these non-therapeutic uses.

Expanding decay-in-storage eligibility by increasing the allowable half-life from 120 to 275 days, enabling safe, cost-effective onsite disposal of longer-lived materials like lutetium-177 metastable (Lu-177m) and cobalt-57 (Co-57).
In its March 2016 report, the ACMUI concluded that no changes to the 700-hour requirement were warranted at that time as they found no evidence that the requirement adversely affected patient access.
Comments must be submitted electronically using https://www.regulations.gov by 11:59 p.m. eastern time on September 10, 2026.
notes: Primary artefact for the signal. Docket NRC-2025-1237, RIN 3150-AL50, 59 pages. Direct fetch exceeds the tool token cap, so the document was retrieved to a local file and the spans above were read from that copy of the live page. The comment period closed on 10 September 2026, three days before the scan date: this is a proposed rule, not settled policy, and the article says so. audit_verbatim_quote_provenance.py cannot reach outbound URLs from the Cowork sandbox, so quotes are recorded as manually verified.

publisher: Federal Register (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services)
title: Medicare hospital outpatient prospective payment and ambulatory surgical centre payment systems, CY 2027 proposed rule, 91 FR 41734
date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-07-07 (on-page standfirst: "A Proposed Rule by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services on 07/07/2026")
key_claim: CMS proposes a CY 2027 diagnostic radiopharmaceutical packaging threshold of $665 per day, trended from the CY 2025 baseline of $630 using the four-quarter moving average PPI for prescription pharmaceuticals to $667.44 and rounded to the nearest $5; the CY 2026 threshold it succeeds is $655. Products above the threshold become separately payable and are paid on arithmetic mean unit cost derived from CY 2025 hospital claims, because CMS still judges manufacturer average sales price data unusable for payment. Products at or below the threshold stay packaged into the procedure payment.
frame_summary: CMS is arguing that a price-indexed per-day cost threshold plus claims-derived mean unit cost remains the defensible way to decide which diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals are paid separately from the procedure bundle.
verbatim_quote: Based on this methodology, we trended the $630 threshold forward and rounded the resulting dollar amount ($667.44) to the nearest $5 increment, which yields a proposed figure of $665 per day for CY 2027.
verbatim_list: In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period, we finalized a technical refinement to the diagnostic radiopharmaceutical packaging threshold methodology and finalized the CY 2026 diagnostic radiopharmaceutical packaging threshold of $655.

HCPCS codes that describe diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals with per day costs that are at or below the proposed diagnostic radiopharmaceutical packaging threshold are proposed to continue to be assigned to a status indicator of "N", indicating packaged payment.
notes: Docket CMS-1850-P, RIN 0938-AV83. Used to establish that Medicare prices radiopharmaceutical doses per day and per unit, not the shielded room, hot lab or staffing the treatment requires. Negative finding recorded during verification: a full-text sweep of the document found no technetium-99m or molybdenum-99 domestic-production add-on language, so no such claim is attributed to it. Direct fetch exceeds the tool token cap; the document was retrieved to a local file and the spans read from that copy. Proposed, not final, at the scan date.

publisher: The Lancet Regional Health - Europe (PubMed Central)
title: Estimation of future patient populations eligible for radioligand therapies in the EU and the UK: a modelling study
key_claim: Modelling with the European Commission Joint Research Centre finds the EU-27 pool theoretically eligible for radioligand therapy rising from 11,000-13,000 in 2025 to roughly 130,000-180,000 by 2035. A utilisation-based scenario puts 17,000-35,000 EU-4 patients treated in 2030, rising to about 37,000 by 2035. The utilisation inputs show the delivery gap directly: 56.7 patients per million population are eligible for PSMA-targeting radioligand therapy in high-income countries against actual utilisation of 14.2 per million for 177Lu-PSMA and 0.3 per million for 225Ac-PSMA. The authors state the expected uptake may overwhelm available treatment capacity even where nuclear medicine infrastructure is well developed.
frame_summary: The authors are arguing that Europe's radioligand-therapy eligible population will outgrow its nuclear medicine delivery capacity within a decade, making access an equity problem that requires coordinated national capacity planning.
verbatim_quote: The expected uptake of RLTs in EU healthcare systems over the coming decade may overwhelm available treatment capacity, even in countries with well-developed nuclear medicine infrastructure.
verbatim_list: Between 2025 and 2035 in the EU-27, the patient pool theoretically eligible for RLTs could increase from 11,000 to 13,000 to approximately 130,000–180,000. A scenario based on preliminary utilisation data suggests that, in the EU-4, 17,000–35,000 patients from this pool could be treated in 2030, increasing to approximately 37,000 patients by 2035.
Treated patients were calculated based on a utilisation per million population of 16.3 for 177Lu-DOTATATE, 14.2 for 177Lu-PSMA, and 0.3 for 225Ac-PSMA for high income countries
Patients eligible for PSMA-targeting RLT were calculated using a rate of eligible patients of 56.7 per million population in high-income countries
Research by WifOR was funded by Novartis Pharma AG. JRC research was covered by the European Commission's Research Framework Programmes budget.
notes: Single permitted structural anchor for this scan: published 4 June 2026, 101 days before scan date, therefore in the 3-6 month band, and the canonical quantification of the eligibility-versus-delivery gap. MATERIAL CONFLICT OF INTEREST, disclosed here and flagged in the delivery message: the lead author is affiliated to Novartis Pharma AG and the WifOR modelling was Novartis-funded; co-authorship with the European Commission Joint Research Centre is what supports the Tier 1 classification. Novartis is the incumbent with the largest commercial interest in radioligand capacity being described as constrained, so the projections are treated as the manufacturer-adjacent upper case rather than as neutral forecast. title: NRC proposes major changes to medical use regulations
key_claim: ACR reports that under the proposed rule licensed facilities would no longer need a licence amendment to add authorised users for diagnostic nuclear medicine under certain Part 35 sections, with licensees verifying and documenting physician qualifications internally and NRC or Agreement State oversight occurring primarily through inspections. The NRC also proposes to expand authorised-user eligibility to certain foreign-trained physicians licensed to practise in the US, and to codify frameworks for mature emerging technologies. A 45-day comment window applies from Federal Register publication.
frame_summary: ACR is arguing that this is a consequential move of qualification gatekeeping from prior regulatory approval to retrospective inspection, and that the radiology profession should organise a response.
verbatim_quote: Among the proposed revisions, licensed facilities would no longer need license amendments to add Authorized Users (AUs) for diagnostic nuclear medicine uses under certain sections of Part 35. Instead, licensees would verify and document physician qualifications internally, with NRC or Agreement State oversight occurring primarily through inspections.
verbatim_list: The NRC also proposes changes to expand AU-eligibility for certain foreign-trained physicians who are licensed to practice medicine in the U.S. if they meet the corresponding training and experience requirements.
plans to accept public comments for 45 days following publication in the Federal Register
notes: Professional-society advocacy item with an interest in how its members' qualification is regulated, so it is used for its reading of the mechanism (prior approval moving to retrospective inspection) while the primary rule text carries the underlying claim.

title: Targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy: advances, investment dynamics, and future directions, part 2
key_claim: The review finds that the practical constraint on expanding radiopharmaceutical therapy programmes and decentralised trial execution is the limited availability of trained nuclear medicine, radiochemistry and radiopharmaceutical-manufacturing professionals rather than molecule supply. Drawing on a commercial clinical-trial database it counts approximately 2,586 active sites worldwide treating patients with radiopharmaceutical therapy as of May 2025. It also notes that vertical integration into radiopharmaceutical infrastructure carries heavy upfront cost and that nuclear-safety compliance and specialised GMP processes now feed directly into asset valuation.
frame_summary: The authors are arguing that value in radiopharmaceutical therapy is increasingly set by who controls infrastructure, supply contracts and trained personnel rather than by molecule differentiation.
verbatim_quote: Limited availability of trained professionals in nuclear medicine, radiochemistry, and radiopharmaceutical manufacturing represents a practical constraint for the expansion of RPT clinical programs and decentralized trial execution.
verbatim_list: Vertical integration demands heavy upfront investment and may lack scale for smaller developers. Regulatory and operational complexities—from nuclear-safety compliance to specialized GMP processes—add to cost and risk, making infrastructure and long-term supply contracts integral to valuation.
indicates that, worldwide, approximately 2,586 active sites are treating patients with RPT as of May 2025.
notes: DATE AMBIGUITY, disclosed: the journal issue metadata and article:published_time both give 1 September 2026 (volume 67, issue 9), which is what is recorded here, but the page footer records online-first publication on 21 May 2026, which would fall in the 3-6 month band and would collide with the structural-anchor allowance already used by the Lancet study. The issue date is recorded because it is the page's own published_time. The site-count figure of approximately 2,586 is drawn by the authors from GlobalData's commercial clinical-trial database, so it is a secondary count. Senior author Ken Herrmann is also the interviewee in the AuntMinnieEurope Q&A used in this scan, so those two sources are not independent on the workforce question.

publisher: World Journal of Nuclear Medicine (PubMed Central)
title: Uneven global distribution of theranostics
date_evidence: EDITORIAL World J Nucl Med. 2026 Jun 15;25(2):101–102. doi: 10.1055/s-0046-1824537 (meta-citation_publication_date: 2026 Jun 15)
key_claim: The editorial reports IAEA estimates that approximately 70% to 80% of global nuclear medicine procedures occur in North America, Europe, Japan and Australia, while regions holding over half the world's population account for a small fraction of theranostic treatments. High-income countries often run 10 to 40 PET scanners per million people against fewer than 1 per million in many low-income countries, and 10 to 20 nuclear medicine physicians per million against fewer than 1 per million in many low- and middle-income countries. It describes a theranostic affordability paradox in which clinical demand and expertise exist but imported isotope costs, fragmented regulatory pathways and thin local production constrain delivery.
frame_summary: The authors are arguing that theranostic delivery capacity is locked to national health spending, isotope infrastructure and trained workforce, so access should be treated as a global health priority rather than a high-income privilege.
verbatim_quote: The IAEA estimated that approximately 70% to 80% of global nuclear medicine procedures occur in North America, Europe, Japan, and Australia, while regions containing over half of the world's population account for only a small fraction of theranostic treatments.
verbatim_list: High-income countries often have 10 to 40 PET scanners per million people, while many low-income countries have fewer than 1 scanner per million, and some have none at all.
Workforce differences are also substantial: High-income countries may have 10 to 20 nuclear medicine physicians per million inhabitants, whereas many LMICs have fewer than 1 per million.
notes: A two-page editorial rather than original research: its ranges are secondary figures attributed to its own references, given without a data table, so they are used as order-of-magnitude context rather than as precise anchors. The page states no conflict of interest. Plain HTTP fetch of the PMC URL returns a reCAPTCHA interstitial; the same exact URL was loaded in a browser pane to read the text, and no CAPTCHA was solved. Do not conflate this editorial with the separate 2025 IAEA-perspective paper in the same journal, which circulates in search snippets with different figures.

title: Q&A with Ken Herrmann: theranostics must move earlier and beyond established targets
key_claim: Ken Herrmann, director of nuclear medicine at University Hospital Essen, argues the field's priorities are moving PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy into earlier treatment lines and expanding beyond prostate and neuroendocrine tumours, which would enlarge the treated population sharply. On workforce he states the recruitment position has improved materially and that his department can now be selective, where workforce planning previously caused sleepless nights. He also notes German-speaking countries are more cautious about radiopharmaceuticals than others.
frame_summary: Herrmann is arguing that what limits theranostics is the quality of clinical evidence and the narrowness of current targets, not staffing.
verbatim_quote: The situation has probably never been better. We are receiving strong applications and can be selective about who joins our department. In the past, workforce planning caused us sleepless nights; that situation has changed.
verbatim_list: One major development is moving established radioligand therapies into earlier treatment lines. Recent evidence on PSMA-targeted therapy represents a significant change for the field.
notes: Used deliberately as counter-evidence on the workforce leg of the signal. Single-expert, single-institution testimony from a leading European academic centre that has just opened a new theranostics centre, so it is a best case and not generalisable to community or lower-income settings. Herrmann is also senior author of the Journal of Nuclear Medicine review used in this scan, so the two sources are not independent.

title: Why community oncology should act now to implement radiopharmaceutical therapies
key_claim: A physician-network operator sets out the licensed-estate checklist for radioligand therapy, a hot lab, shielded infusion rooms and bathrooms, a radioactive materials licence, an authorised user and a certified nuclear medicine technologist, then argues it is surmountable in community settings at roughly $250,000 of startup cost for a small programme, recoverable within a year at margins around 14% at Medicare rates. It recommends contract technologists for the one or two days a week a centre runs the therapy rather than full-time staffing.
frame_summary: The network is arguing that the licensed-estate barrier is a solvable capital and contracting problem, so community oncology should build the capability now rather than cede it to academic centres.
verbatim_quote: Radiopharmaceuticals offer a compelling opportunity, with current margins around 14% at Medicare rates. Startup costs for a basic program can be relatively modest – approximately $250,000 for a small, well-designed setup – and can be recouped quickly with consistent patient volume.
verbatim_list: Facilities need a "hot lab" to receive and handle radioactive materials, as well as shielded infusion rooms and bathrooms to ensure the safety of patients and staff. Practices must also obtain a radioactive materials license and comply with all associated regulations.
Radiopharmaceuticals are not fundamentally new or overly complex and can be safely administered in community settings with the appropriate precautions.
notes: Vendor-side corroboration only, never an anchor. American Oncology Network sells the build-and-operate service it describes, so both the $250,000 figure and the not-overly-complex claim are self-serving; they are used deliberately as the strongest form of the counter-argument rather than as independent validation.
